paragraphs: Training a shallow ReLU network involves deciding which neurons activate on which training examples. The paper separates this difficult optimization problem into a combinatorial search over activation patterns and a constrained convex problem once those patterns are fixed. This makes the discrete choices inside network training explicit.

The authors represent feasible activation patterns using a geometric object called a zonotope. Its vertices correspond to the possible activation configurations, providing a way to analyze training through geometry. They use this connection to study how changes in the training data affect the best achievable loss and to examine strategies for selecting promising vertices.

This perspective also explains a benefit of overparameterization: a randomly selected vertex becomes more likely to contain a good solution. The paper introduces a polynomial-time vertex-selection procedure that provably includes the global optimum when using twice the minimum parameter count needed to fit the data. It also reports that a greedy local search over vertices outperforms gradient descent on underparameterized problems.
neurips-2022-a-combinatorial-perspective.tldr: A geometric view of ReLU activation patterns yields new optimization guarantees and a greedy search method that improves training on underparameterized problems.

paragraphs: The paper studies limits on how accurately one family of functions can represent another. For neural networks, this asks what approximation error remains unavoidable given the network's expressive capacity. The authors first address the broader mathematical problem before applying their result to particular network families.

Their lower bound measures error in an Lp norm, for any p at least one and any probability measure. It depends on three properties: how many distinguishable functions the target family contains, the range of their values, and a capacity measure called the fat-shattering dimension of the approximating family. This connects the richness of the targets with the representational resources available to approximate them.

The authors apply the bound to feedforward networks with piecewise-polynomial components, considering Hölder balls and multivariate monotonic functions as targets. Their lower bounds match known or new upper bounds up to logarithmic factors. The results also clarify relationships between Lp approximation and approximation measured by the largest error anywhere, resolving an open question identified in the abstract.
neurips-2022-a-general-approximation-low.tldr: A general approximation lower bound connects target-function complexity with model capacity and establishes near-matching limits for several neural-network approximation problems.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which examples to send for annotation so that a model can learn with fewer labels. This is particularly difficult when the annotation budget is very small. The paper builds on improved representations from representation learning and self-supervised learning, whose geometry contains useful information about relationships among examples.

The proposed algorithm, ProbCover, treats annotation selection as a coverage problem. It seeks a subset that maximizes Probability Coverage, using the representation space to guide the choice of examples. The authors also give a dual interpretation of this formulation that leads toward strategies for larger annotation budgets and connects to existing approaches such as Coreset.

Experiments on several image-recognition benchmarks show improved performance over the state of the art in the low-budget setting. The gains are especially useful when combined with semi-supervised learning, which also uses unlabeled examples. In the reported experiments, this combination allows leading semi-supervised methods to match fully supervised performance while requiring substantially fewer labels.
neurips-2022-active-learning-through-a-c.tldr: ProbCover selects examples for labeling by maximizing coverage in representation space, improving active learning when annotation budgets are small.

paragraphs: The paper studies how independently learning players can approach a coarse correlated equilibrium in a general game. Its algorithm, Clairvoyant Multiplicative Weights Updates, changes the information used in an otherwise familiar strategy update: players calculate their new strategies using payoffs associated with the next strategies rather than the current ones.

This apparent look into the future is formulated as a fixed-point computation. The ideal update achieves regret bounded by ln(m)/η, where m is the number of actions and η is the step size. The computational concern is that each player's next strategy depends on the others' next strategies, so the updates must be mutually consistent.

The authors show that a contraction map computes these updates with linear convergence when η is at most 1/((n−1)V), for n players and payoff range [0,V]. Their implementation produces an uncoupled learning process with a sparse subsequence enjoying bounded regret. It yields a coarse-correlated-equilibrium convergence rate of O(nV log(m) log(T)/T), improving the previous state of the art reported in the abstract.
neurips-2022-beyond-time-average-converg.tldr: A future-dependent multiplicative-weights update can be implemented through a contraction map to improve equilibrium convergence under a stated step-size condition.

paragraphs: Sequential games can be converted into normal-form games, making established learning methods available. The obstacle is computational: this conversion can expand the game's representation exponentially. The paper investigates when the benefits of a normal-form algorithm called Phi-Hedge can be retained without paying that exponential cost.

The authors establish a connection between Phi-Hedge and online mirror descent operating on extensive-form games with suitable dilated regularizers. In the settings they analyze, the algorithms are equivalent and run in polynomial time. These settings cover learning Nash equilibria in zero-sum games, normal-form coarse correlated equilibria, and extensive-form correlated equilibria.

The connection also provides a route to new algorithms by modifying the log-partition function. Using balancing techniques, the authors obtain an extensive-form-correlated-equilibrium regret bound of approximately √(XAT), with logarithmic factors suppressed, under bandit feedback. Here X counts information sets, A counts actions, and T counts episodes. They identify this as the first such rate to their knowledge and show that it matches the information-theoretic lower bound up to the suppressed factors.
neurips-2022-efficient-phi-regret-minimi.tldr: An equivalence with online mirror descent makes Phi-Hedge efficient in several sequential-game settings and yields a near-optimal bandit-feedback regret bound.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning systems repeatedly run environments to collect experience for training. Even when other parts of the training system are optimized, generating this experience can remain the slowest stage. EnvPool targets that bottleneck through an execution engine designed to run many environments in parallel.

The reported improvements span laptops, workstations, and high-end machines. On a high-end system, EnvPool reaches one million frames per second for Atari environment execution and three million for MuJoCo. On a laptop, it runs at 2.8 times the speed of the Python subprocess approach. These figures describe environment simulation, the specific system component the paper aims to accelerate.

The authors also report compatibility with existing reinforcement-learning libraries, including CleanRL, rl_games, and DeepMind Acme. This matters because a faster execution engine can become part of established training workflows. Example runs train agents to play Atari Pong and MuJoCo Ant in five minutes on a laptop, illustrating the potential for faster experimental iteration.
neurips-2022-envpool-a-highly-parallel-r.tldr: EnvPool accelerates parallel reinforcement-learning environment execution across hardware scales and integrates with existing training libraries.

paragraphs: A model can make confident predictions even when its learned knowledge does not justify that confidence. Ensembles help estimate this epistemic uncertainty by combining multiple models, but storing and training separate deep networks can be expensive. The paper explores how to obtain useful ensemble diversity within a single network.

FiLM-Ensemble adapts feature-wise linear modulation, a technique originally developed to separate tasks in multitask learning. It modulates the activations of one deep network to produce an implicit ensemble. The authors show that this produces diverse ensemble behavior and well-calibrated estimates of epistemic uncertainty, with relatively little computational overhead.

In the reported experiments, FiLM-Ensemble outperforms other implicit ensemble methods. Its performance approaches the explicit ensemble used as the upper benchmark and sometimes exceeds it, while requiring only a fraction of the memory. The practical contribution is a way to bring ensemble-style uncertainty estimates into settings where keeping multiple complete networks would impose a substantial resource burden.
neurips-2022-film-ensemble-probabilistic.tldr: FiLM-Ensemble modulates a single network's activations to obtain diverse predictions and calibrated uncertainty at substantially lower memory cost than explicit ensembles.

paragraphs: Physical backdoors use real objects as triggers for a model's misclassification. Studying them requires images where candidate trigger objects appear alongside relevant target objects, and manually collecting these images takes considerable work. The paper asks whether suitable combinations already exist in widely available image datasets.

The authors propose a scalable method for finding subsets containing potential physical triggers and identifying the classes those triggers could poison. Carefully relabeling the selected images turns them into training data for backdoor research. The naturally occurring element is the co-location of objects in existing images; the attack-training dataset is constructed through the subsequent selection and relabeling.

The method successfully identifies such subsets in widely available datasets. Models trained using them exhibit behavior equivalent to models trained on manually curated physical-backdoor datasets in the reported study. This makes existing image collections a useful resource for investigating a type of backdoor that the abstract describes as resistant to most defenses designed for digital trigger patterns.
neurips-2022-finding-naturally-occurring.tldr: The paper finds existing images with useful object co-occurrences and turns selected, relabeled subsets into datasets for physical-backdoor research.

paragraphs: Embedding models represent items as latent vectors that can support modeling and prediction tasks. The paper addresses a restriction of many such models: they are designed around a single type of observed data. When information about an item comes in several forms, that restriction limits what the representation-learning method can incorporate.

The authors propose a Gaussian copula embedding model for this heterogeneous setting. Its central purpose is to learn item representations while incorporating different types of observations within the same model. The abstract reports that the resulting embeddings are robust, making the ability to combine observations part of a broader claim about representation quality.

The evaluation covers multiple scenarios and reports improvements over competing models in both modeling quality and task performance. These two findings concern different uses of the learned representations: describing the observed data and supporting a task built on those representations. Together, they support the proposed model as an effective approach to heterogeneous embedding problems in the settings studied.
neurips-2022-gaussian-copula-embeddings-.tldr: Gaussian copula embeddings combine heterogeneous observations into robust item representations and outperform competing models in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Reasoning prompts often teach language models how to answer by supplying examples with intermediate steps. This paper tests a simpler intervention: adding “Let's think step by step” before the answer, without providing worked examples. The resulting approach, Zero-shot-CoT, uses the same prompt template across different reasoning tasks.

The experiments cover arithmetic, symbolic reasoning, and other logical tasks. With text-davinci-002, accuracy rises from 17.7% to 78.7% on MultiArith and from 10.4% to 40.7% on GSM8K. The authors also report improvements of similar magnitude with the 540-billion-parameter PaLM model. These results show that a brief instruction can substantially change measured reasoning performance in the tested models.

The broader implication is that useful capabilities may remain hidden when evaluation relies on an ordinary zero-shot prompt. The authors interpret the prompt's versatility as evidence suggesting broader, underexplored reasoning capabilities, rather than establishing universal reasoning ability. Their work motivates examining what pretrained models can already do with simple prompting before investing in task-specific examples or fine-tuning data.
neurips-2022-large-language-models-are-z.tldr: A simple step-by-step instruction substantially improves zero-shot reasoning performance across several benchmarks without supplying worked examples.

paragraphs: Graph prediction can face distribution shifts in both node attributes and graph structure. This makes it difficult to determine which information should remain reliable when the data changes. Obtaining environment or domain partitions, which many generalization methods require, can also be expensive for graph datasets.

CIGA addresses this problem by using causal models to characterize potential graph shifts. Its analysis identifies a condition for out-of-distribution generalization: prediction should focus on subgraphs containing the most information about the causes of labels. The method then uses an information-theoretic objective to extract subgraphs that preserve as much invariant information within each class as possible.

The robustness claim is tied to the causal characterization and the desired informative subgraphs. Within that framework, learning from those subgraphs is immune to the modeled shifts. Experiments on 16 synthetic and real-world datasets, including DrugOOD for drug-discovery-related prediction, report superior out-of-distribution performance. The findings connect a theoretical criterion for stable prediction with a concrete objective for selecting graph information.
neurips-2022-learning-causally-invariant.tldr: CIGA uses causal modeling and an information-theoretic objective to select graph substructures intended to remain predictive under distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Many graph neural networks construct node representations by exchanging information between immediate neighbors at each layer. Graph Transformers can consider connections beyond the original sparse graph, making them candidates for tasks involving distant interactions. Yet existing benchmarks often favor conventional message-passing models enhanced with features such as positional representations.

The paper introduces the Long Range Graph Benchmark to make those distant dependencies more central to evaluation. It contains five datasets: PascalVOC-SP, COCO-SP, PCQM-Contact, Peptides-func, and Peptides-struct. The authors argue that strong performance on these tasks calls for reasoning about long-range interactions, creating a more targeted setting for comparing relevant architectures.

Experiments compare baseline graph neural networks with Graph Transformer models. Models that capture long-range dependencies perform significantly better on the proposed tasks. This supports the benchmark's usefulness for studying that capability, while keeping the conclusion specific to the evaluated tasks. The contribution is an evaluation resource that helps reveal benefits which may be less visible on established graph benchmarks.
neurips-2022-long-range-graph-benchmark-.tldr: LRGB introduces five graph datasets on which models capturing long-range dependencies show a clear performance advantage.

paragraphs: A model trained across several source domains may still struggle with the particular characteristics of a new target domain. Meta-DMoE addresses this through unsupervised adaptation at test time. Instead of placing all source knowledge in one model, it trains separate experts on different domains so that each can retain specialized knowledge.

For a target domain, a small collection of unlabeled examples queries these experts. A transformer-based aggregator examines relationships among their domain knowledge and combines their outputs into a supervision signal. A student prediction network then adapts to the target using that signal. This design draws on the stated relationship between the source and target domains.

Meta-learning trains the aggregator to transfer useful knowledge and prepares the student for rapid adaptation. The reported experiments outperform the state of the art and support the effectiveness of the individual components. The approach therefore connects source specialization with target-specific adaptation: expert knowledge is combined in response to the new domain rather than applied identically to every unseen domain.
neurips-2022-meta-dmoe-adapting-to-domai.tldr: Meta-DMoE adapts a student model to a new domain using unlabeled examples and meta-learned distillation from specialized source-domain experts.

paragraphs: Preference-based reinforcement learning uses human comparisons to guide behavior, reducing the need to hand-design a reward function. Because human feedback can be scarce, learning effectively from a small number of preferences is central to this approach. Meta-Reward-Net focuses on improving how those preferences shape reward and policy learning.

The method uses a two-level optimization process. At the inner level, it learns the policy and the Q-function, which evaluates actions. At the outer level, it adjusts the reward function according to how well the Q-function performs on the preference data. This makes the quality of the learned action evaluation a target for reward learning.

Experiments on simulated robotic manipulation and locomotion tasks report stronger performance than prior methods when preference labels are few, along with improved data efficiency. Ablation studies also find a more accurate Q-function and particular advantages when little human feedback is available. These findings support coordinating reward learning with downstream learning performance as a way to make scarce preferences more useful.
neurips-2022-meta-reward-net-implicitly-.tldr: Meta-Reward-Net uses two-level optimization to learn rewards through Q-function performance, improving reinforcement learning with limited preference feedback.

paragraphs: Online learning evaluates a sequence of decisions through regret, comparing accumulated performance with a reference choice. Obtaining useful guarantees is difficult when the objectives are non-convex. This paper studies a structured setting where changing the parameterization connects non-convex gradient descent with convex mirror descent.

Under specified geometric and smoothness conditions, the authors show that discrete online gradient descent approximately follows the corresponding convex mirror-descent algorithm. Earlier work had established an exact relationship for continuous-time dynamics. The unresolved issue was whether that relationship could support guarantees for algorithms taking discrete steps, as actual iterative procedures do.

The paper resolves this issue in the analyzed setting by proving an O(T^(2/3)) regret bound over T rounds. Since this grows more slowly than T, regret per round decreases with a longer sequence. The result depends on the stated conditions and reparameterization. Its methodological contribution is an algorithmic equivalence argument that transfers useful convex-optimization structure to a class of non-convex online problems.
neurips-2022-non-convex-online-learning-.tldr: Under geometric and smoothness conditions, approximate equivalence with convex mirror descent gives non-convex online gradient descent an O(T^(2/3)) regret guarantee.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether Gaussian process regression can learn efficiently when a target function has compositional structure. Such structure matters because the arrangement of simpler components can affect which model families learn well. The authors prove that deep Gaussian process priors can outperform Gaussian process priors for targets of this kind.

Their analysis uses information-theoretic lower bounds on posterior contraction rates in a continuous regression model. A contraction rate describes how quickly the posterior concentrates around the true function as the sample size grows. A lower bound establishes a limit on that learning speed, rather than merely describing the performance of one fitted example.

For generalized additive target functions, the posterior from any mean-zero Gaussian process recovers the truth more slowly than the minimax rate. The gap is polynomial in the sample size, giving a substantive separation from the best achievable rate. This result identifies a theoretical advantage that deep priors can have when the target's compositional structure is central to the regression problem.
neurips-2022-on-the-inability-of-gaussia.tldr: The paper proves a polynomial learning-rate disadvantage for mean-zero Gaussian process priors on generalized additive targets, establishing a possible advantage for deep priors.

paragraphs: A backdoored neural network can behave normally on ordinary inputs but predict an attacker's target class when a trigger appears. One defensive strategy is to purify the trained model. Existing purification methods can become much less effective when only a small amount of original training data is available.

Adversarial Weight Masking addresses this data constraint through a min-max optimization problem. It first adversarially recovers perturbation patterns associated with non-robust behavior. It then applies soft masks to network weights that are sensitive to those patterns. This connects the search for problematic behavior directly to a mechanism for reducing the influence of the weights involved.

The authors present the method as capable of erasing backdoors even in a one-shot setting. Evaluations on several benchmark datasets suggest substantial improvements in purification over other state-of-the-art methods across different amounts of available training data. The reported findings make the method particularly relevant to model repair when access to the original training collection is severely restricted.
neurips-2022-one-shot-neural-backdoor-er.tldr: Adversarial Weight Masking recovers problematic perturbations and suppresses sensitive weights to improve backdoor removal with very limited training data.

paragraphs: Scaling laws aim to predict how model performance changes as training grows in size or duration. The paper argues that evaluating these laws should focus on how well they predict beyond the observations used to fit them. A close fit to existing measurements does not by itself establish that a forecast will be accurate.

The authors propose using extrapolation loss as the evaluation criterion and give a recipe for estimating scaling-law parameters from learning curves. This aligns parameter estimation and evaluation with the practical purpose of a scaling law: anticipating the benefit of larger training runs. The emphasis is on the reliability of the prediction beyond the fitted range.

Across several architecture families, the method extrapolates more accurately than previous approaches in image classification, neural machine translation, language modeling, and BIG-Bench tasks. The authors also release a dataset comprising 90 evaluation tasks. Together, the estimation procedure and benchmark provide a basis for comparing scaling forecasts across a broader collection of problems.
neurips-2022-revisiting-neural-scaling-l.tldr: The paper improves scaling-law estimation by emphasizing extrapolation accuracy and introduces a 90-task benchmark for evaluating these forecasts.

paragraphs: Creating a large virtual world requires generated views to agree about a shared three-dimensional scene. SGAM tackles this challenge by combining generative sensor modeling with 3D reconstruction. Its goal is to extend scene generation over large spaces while maintaining realistic appearance and globally consistent geometry.

The method follows an autoregressive process: at each step, it generates sensor data from a new viewpoint and builds a 3D map. Given a camera trajectory, it repeats this coupled generation-and-mapping operation for thousands of steps. Training uses RGB-D sequences, which provide color and depth observations, without requiring access to the complete structure of the scene.

Experiments on CLEVER and GoogleEarth report realistic, consistent, and geometrically plausible generated scenes that compare favorably with existing view-synthesis methods. The resulting scenes are also compatible with interactive environments and rendering engines. The contribution is therefore both a way to extend generation across many viewpoints and a way to produce a mapped world usable beyond the generation process itself.
neurips-2022-sgam-building-a-virtual-3d-.tldr: SGAM repeatedly generates new-view sensor data and reconstructs a 3D map to build large, consistent virtual worlds from RGB-D training sequences.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models scale neural networks by routing data to selected experts. In distributed training, those routing decisions also determine communication across the hardware network. The paper argues that existing dispatch patterns do not fully exploit heterogeneous network environments, leaving useful system performance untapped.

TA-MoE makes routing sensitive to the network topology. The authors model communication, express dispatch as an optimization objective, and obtain approximate dispatch patterns for different topologies. They then introduce an auxiliary loss that encourages data routing to fit the underlying network. This links model training decisions with the communication costs imposed by the hardware.

Across the evaluated hardware and model configurations, TA-MoE improves training performance without sacrificing model accuracy. Reported speed improvements are roughly 1.01–1.61 times over DeepSpeed-MoE, 1.01–4.77 times over FastMoE, and 1.25–1.54 times over FasterMoE. The ranges show that the benefit varies by configuration, while supporting topology-aware routing as a useful component of large-scale mixture-of-experts training.
neurips-2022-ta-moe-topology-aware-large.tldr: TA-MoE adapts expert routing to network topology, improving distributed training speed across tested configurations without sacrificing accuracy.

paragraphs: Prior work suggests that training only some network parameters can match full-training performance when information from an already trained model is available. The harder question is how to decide what to train without that look-ahead information. This paper approaches the decision at the level of entire neurons.

The proposed criterion is neuronal equilibrium. A neuron is considered at equilibrium when it has learned a particular input-output relationship, and its updates can then be halted. A neuron that has not reached equilibrium continues to have its parameters updated. This makes the neuron's learned behavior the basis for deciding whether further change is needed.

The authors test the approach across different state-of-the-art learning strategies and tasks, reporting evidence that validates the equilibrium concept. They also observe that neuronal equilibrium depends on the learning setup. That finding matters for interpreting the method: whether a neuron should keep updating is connected to the particular training process, rather than being a fixed property shared across all uses of the neuron.
neurips-2022-to-update-or-not-to-update-.tldr: The paper uses neuronal equilibrium to decide when to halt or continue neuron updates, finding that equilibrium depends on the learning setup.

paragraphs: Neural agents can learn communication systems by optimizing success on a shared task. This paper adds two other pressures: how informative their messages are and how complex their communication system becomes. The motivation comes from information-bottleneck accounts of human language, which balance expressive information against lexicon complexity.

The proposed VQ-VIB method trains agents to encode inputs as discrete signals embedded in a continuous space. The authors evaluate it in multi-agent reinforcement learning and color-reference games. Agents adapt to changing communication needs, and their communication in the color domain aligns with human languages. Their learned embedding spaces also exhibit meaningful semantics grounded in perception.

Encouraging informativeness improves convergence speed and task utility both for VQ-VIB and for earlier symbolic-communication architectures in the reported evaluations. VQ-VIB achieves higher utility at a given complexity. These findings support treating communication as a balance among several objectives, while the suggestion that the framework may help human-agent interaction remains a potential application.
neurips-2022-trading-off-utility-informa.tldr: VQ-VIB balances task utility, informativeness, and communication complexity to help neural agents learn effective and semantically meaningful signals.

paragraphs: A classifier can identify useful patterns while remaining too confident about its predictions. This paper addresses that problem in multiclass classification by changing how the model is trained. The goal is to obtain more dependable uncertainty estimates while preserving predictive power.

The training loss draws inspiration from conformal inference and uses held-out data to quantify model uncertainty. By making uncertainty part of the optimization objective, the method seeks to reduce overconfidence during learning. The authors then apply exact calibration using held-out data to construct conformal prediction sets, which can contain several candidate labels.

Experiments on synthetic and real data show that the method can produce smaller prediction sets with higher conditional coverage than state-of-the-art alternatives. Smaller sets give more specific answers, while the reported coverage improvement concerns how reliably those sets include the correct label under conditioning. Achieving both in the experiments suggests that uncertainty-aware training can improve the usefulness of the calibrated output without sacrificing the classifier's predictive power.
neurips-2022-training-uncertainty-aware-.tldr: A conformal-inspired training loss reduces classifier overconfidence and can yield smaller calibrated prediction sets with higher conditional coverage.

paragraphs: Diffusion autoencoders learn image representations by training an encoder together with a diffusion decoder that reconstructs images. Training the diffusion model from scratch is costly. PDAE instead adapts existing pretrained diffusion models into reconstruction decoders, aiming to reuse their capabilities for more efficient representation learning.

The authors attribute reconstruction failure to information lost during the forward diffusion process. This creates a gap between the model's predicted posterior mean and the true mean. Inspired by an interpretation of classifier guidance as an additional mean shift, they train a model to predict a corrective shift from the encoded image representation.

Learning to fill this gap pushes the encoder to retain information needed for reconstruction. PDAE also reuses part of the pretrained diffusion network and changes the weighting of the diffusion loss. The abstract reports better training efficiency and performance than Diff-AE, with extensive experiments supporting effectiveness and flexibility. The central contribution is a reconstruction-driven way to learn representations from diffusion models that are already trained.
neurips-2022-unsupervised-representation.tldr: PDAE learns image representations by predicting reconstruction corrections for pretrained diffusion models, improving efficiency and performance over Diff-AE.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a bandit problem where an action's reward is the sum of several random outcomes, but the action changes only some of them. Marketing and recommendation provide motivating examples: outcomes may correspond to individual customers, while an intervention affects only a subset. After each action, the learner observes every component outcome.

The proposed algorithms estimate each action's uplift relative to a baseline and use upper-confidence-bound-style decision rules. This takes advantage of the distinction between outcomes an action changes and outcomes it leaves unaffected. The authors study several variants, including cases where the baseline and the identities of the affected variables are unknown.

For all these variants, the paper proves sublinear regret, meaning that accumulated regret grows more slowly than the number of decisions. It also provides lower bounds supporting the necessity of its modeling assumptions. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show benefits over policies that ignore this structure, supporting explicit uplift estimation when the problem has the specified component-level feedback.
neurips-2022-uplifting-bandits-c3d92e7c7.tldr: Uplifting bandits exploit actions' effects on subsets of observed reward components to learn baseline-relative improvements with sublinear regret.
